extracted.intended_audience: readers and researchers interested in comparative/higher education and university governance (policymakers, historians, educators)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the evaluative criteria and institutional standards the chapter uses to describe, judge, and compare universities and colleges (organization, character, resources, teaching, social role).

rubrics_metrics.name: Student conduct and discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: “The conduct of the students is generally good. Intoxication, gaming, or other vices are rare, those who come to work, as the vast majority do, being little prone to such faults; it is only in a few universities situate in or near large cities and resorted to by the sons of the rich that they give serious trouble.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incidence of intoxication, gaming and other vices, and the degree to which student behaviour causes trouble for the President and Faculty, as indicators of institutional discipline. Note caveat: athletic passions (baseball, football, rowing) can create strong cults of personality around athletes that affect campus life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazing/rushing and dormitory order
rubrics_metrics.description: “Order which the authorities have to deal with arise in dormitories from the practice of 'hazing'… Sophomores and freshmen used to have a whimsical habit of meeting one another in dense masses… This is called 'rushing.' Hazing has diminished of late years.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the prevalence and severity of hazing/rushing rituals and their impact on campus order and safety. Observe historical/structural mitigations (e.g., admission of women reduced rushing) and whether institutions curb such practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek-letter fraternities (social organisations)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Greek letter societies… are clubs or fraternities of students… possessing in each a sort of club house… New members are admitted by the votes of the Chapter… They are, so far as I know, always non-political…and one is told that they allow no intoxicants to be kept in their buildings or used at the feasts they provide. They are… deemed a valuable part of the university system, not so much because they cultivate intellectual life as on account of their social influence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence, scale (fraction of student body), governance (Chapter admission), rules (non-political, no intoxicants), facilities (club house), and social influence (lifelong bonds, alumni networks). Consider both benefits (social cohesion, alumni support) and limits (less emphasis on intellectual cultivation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Honorary/literary societies as merit indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: “There exist a few honorary societies into which students are elected in virtue of purely literary or scientific acquirements… The oldest and most famous is called the ΦΒΚ (Phi Beta Kappa) … and exists in many of the leading universities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence and activity of honorary societies (e.g., Phi Beta Kappa) signal recognition of scholarly attainment; use membership selection by academic merit as a quality marker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denominational character and religious affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: “A good many of the American universities, and indeed a majority of the smaller colleges, are denominational… this term… means that they have been founded by or in connection with a particular church… except as regards the Roman Catholic institutions, there is seldom any exclusion of teachers, and never of students… and one is told that they allow no sectarian cast to the instruction (except in theological departments).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an institution is denominational, how that affiliation affects hiring/admissions, whether instruction is sectarian (notably only theological departments), and the extent to which denominational roots shape governance or culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious services / chapel attendance policy
rubrics_metrics.description: “In all the older universities… there is a chapel in which religious services are regularly held… In most institutions every student, unless… he has some conscientious objection, is expected to attend. The service seldom or never contains anything of a sectarian character… Attendance at the college chapel, formerly compulsory, is now voluntary [at Harvard]… short morning daily services with extempore prayers are conducted by the chaplains, who are eminent ministers of different denominations, serving in turn.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the organization (compulsory vs voluntary), character (sectarian vs unsectarian), frequency (daily, weekly), and inclusivity (conducted by clergy of various denominations) of religious services as indicators of the institution's religious ethos and student obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion should be unsectarian in character
rubrics_metrics.description: “The more prevalent view is that a university ought to be in a general sense religious without being sectarian.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional policies and practice against the ideal of fostering religious sentiment or moral instruction without imposing sectarian doctrine; evaluate arrangements made to include multiple denominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of higher education for women (coeducation vs separate colleges)
rubrics_metrics.description: “These efforts have chiefly flowed in two channels. One is the admission of women to co-education with men… In the Eastern States the tendency has been to establish 'universities or colleges exclusively for women'… The best known… are Vassar, Wellesley, Smith, Mount Holyoke, Bryn Mawr.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether women are admitted to coeducation or taught in separate women's colleges, living arrangements (separate lodging), classroom interactions (sometimes separate seating), and measures of success: student numbers, faculty makeup, incomes, degree conferrals, and perceived quality of teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of coeducation on academic culture
rubrics_metrics.description: “The effect on the manners and general tone of the students was excellent… the young men sometimes find the competition of the girls rather severe, and call them 'study machines'… they are more eager, and less addicted to sports or to mere lounging.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing coeducation, consider its social and pedagogical effects: changes in manners, academic competition, participation in sports, and campus culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional classification: 'true university' vs pretentious school
rubrics_metrics.description: “In America the universities are not… a well-defined class of institutions. Not only is the distance between the best and the worst greater… but the gradations… are so imperceptible that one can nowhere draw a line and say that here the true university stops and the pretentious school begins.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structural and performance features (breadth and depth of instruction, research/professional trainings, resources) rather than mere external seeming to classify institutions. Beware of institutions that have the 'skeleton plan' of a university but perform as raw schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key development metrics for universities
rubrics_metrics.description: “The development of the already existing Universities and Colleges goes on with undiminishing speed. It is seen in four directions: additions to the endowments, the creation of new departments, the raising of salaries paid to teachers, and an increase in the number of students.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure institutional growth and health by tracking endowment increases, new departments/professional schools created, faculty compensation levels, and student enrolment growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision and expansion of applied science and technical education
rubrics_metrics.description: “The march of scientific discovery has led to an enormous increase in the applications of science to productive industry… the teaching of applied science has been provided on a scale undreamed of… a host of independent or affiliated scientific schools and technical institutes have sprung up.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence and scale of applied science/technical departments and affiliated institutes; note placement (often in cities) and the role of agricultural colleges with experimental farms in rural education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth of professional schools (medicine, dentistry, law)
rubrics_metrics.description: “These new developments, including the enlargement of the professional schools (medicine, dentistry, and law) attached to the Universities, have of course led to large increases in the teaching staff.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider enlargement and quality of professional schools as indicators of an institution's maturity and ability to meet societal needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty numbers, remuneration, and retirement provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The number of professors and instructors of all kinds rose from 7,918 in 1889 to 22,359 in 1909. There has also been a tendency to raise the salaries of the teachers… the remuneration allotted to presidents and teachers of all grades remains small when compared… with the attainments now expected and… cost of living. Mr. Andrew Carnegie has created a fund… for the purpose of providing retiring allowances for professors… the most important… that they are not to be under the control of any particular sect or denomination.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use faculty growth, average and maximum salaries, and availability of retirement/retiring allowances as measures of institutional investment in academic staff. Note disparities (many institutions pay low averages) and the influence of private funds in setting unofficial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of philanthropic funds on standards
rubrics_metrics.description: “The creation of this fund [Carnegie retiring allowances] has had the incidental result of tending to establish, not without protests and complaints, a sort of unofficial standard of excellence for colleges.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how external philanthropic conditions and eligibility criteria influence institutional behaviour and create de facto standards of excellence (e.g., requirements for non-sectarian status to receive benefits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity vs quality — enrolments and resources versus instructional quality
rubrics_metrics.description: “The fact remains that the institutions are there and the students are there. The revenues grow: the attendance grows. Quantity at least has been obtained. Of quality I shall speak later.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate easily measured growth (student numbers, revenues, endowments) from harder-to-measure instructional quality; avoid equating size with educational excellence without further evidence of teaching and research standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and value of small denominational colleges in rural districts
rubrics_metrics.description: “The European observer… conceives that his American friends may not duly realize the services which these small colleges have performed in the rural districts… They get hold of a multitude of poor men… They set learning in a visible form… They give the chance of rising… to many a strong and earnest nature… In some of these smaller Western colleges one finds today men of great ability and great attainments.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the higher-education ecosystem, account for small colleges' social reach, accessibility for the rural and poor, and their potential to develop into stronger institutions or to seed regional educational improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of adequate university apparatus (libraries, museums, laboratories)
rubrics_metrics.description: “They alleged that the unsectarian character of the State establishments… made them less capable of giving a moral and religious training. But… it was more and more clearly seen that the small colleges would not, for want of funds, provide the various appliances — libraries, museums, laboratories, and so forth — which universities need.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the availability of essential academic infrastructure (libraries, museums, labs, experimental farms) as criteria distinguishing full-scale universities from weaker colleges; scarcity of such appliances argues for concentration of resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proliferation of degree-granting bodies and dilution of degree value
rubrics_metrics.description: “Educational reformers are apt to deplore the absence of control. They complain of the multiplication of degree-giving bodies, and consequent lowering of the worth of a degree.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess regulatory controls on degree-granting authority and the potential negative effect of uncontrolled proliferation on the perceived worth and standards of degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/institutional rigidity of endowments
rubrics_metrics.description: “The law of most American States has not yet recognized the necessity of providing proper methods for setting aside the dispositions made by founders when circumstances change or their regulations prove unsuitable. Endowments… will become a very doubtful blessing unless this question is boldly dealt with.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider legal flexibility (or lack thereof) for redirecting or modifying endowment terms as a factor in an institution’s ability to adapt to changing educational needs; rigid founding dispositions can hamper institutional development.
